teaching.causalExplanation: About half. The same energy, shared among twice as many particles, gives each one only about half as much extra. That's the difference between heat and temperature. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Temperature is how hot something is, and it depends on the average energy of the particles. So the rise depends on how much heat went in, and on how much stuff it had to warm. It also depends on what the stuff is. Specific heat capacity, c, is the energy needed to warm one gram of a substance by one degree. For water it's four point one eight joules per gram per degree. Copper needs only about zero point three nine joules. The data sheet writes water's value per kilogram, four point one eight times ten to the three joules per kilogram per kelvin. That's the same value, written per gram. Now build the formula. One gram of water, warmed by one degree, takes four point one eight joules. Two hundred grams takes two hundred times as much. And warming it by eleven point seven degrees takes eleven point seven times that again. So the heat is the mass, times the specific heat capacity, times the temperature change. q equals m c delta T.

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "How can a calorimeter turn a temperature rise into heat transfer?" The answer, in order: the rise depends on the heat, the mass warmed and the material (1 to 3); multiplying them gives q = mcΔT (4, 5); every quantity in it belongs to the material that warmed (6 to 9); the container helps get the heat into that material (10); q is the surroundings' gain, so the reaction's heat change is the same size with the opposite sign (11); the result is only as good as the assumption that all the heat reached the liquid (12).
